conclusion.content: The real-space termination of a honeycomb nanoribbon—that is, the specific choice of bulk unit cell used to define the periodic Bloch Hamiltonian—determines whether the ribbon Bloch Hamiltonian admits the chiral spectral symmetry $\Gamma h(k)\Gamma^{-1}=-h(k)$; when the chosen termination yields a Bloch Hamiltonian with this chiral symmetry the multiband Zak phase across the hybridization gap is quantized and produces pinned end states, whereas terminations that break the chiral symmetry give non-quantized Zak phases and either produce split (unpinned) end-localized states or no in-gap end states at all for the same bulk parameter set. By selecting different terminations at the two physical ends of a finite ribbon it is possible to realize a single localized end mode confined to one termination (a localized monomode) because one end can be in the symmetry-respecting termination class while the other is not.

steps.reasoning: Define the conceptual relation between termination and bulk unit cell: in a crystalline tight-binding description, the bulk Bloch Hamiltonian corresponds to a specific choice of unit cell; an open system must terminate in full copies of that same unit cell for bulk topological invariants computed from the Bloch Hamiltonian to directly dictate boundary phenomena. Thus "termination" refers to the physical arrangement of atoms at the ribbon ends and is equivalent to the choice of bulk unit cell used to compute bulk invariants.

Explain how different terminations change the explicit Bloch Hamiltonian even while leaving eigenvalues invariant: while eigenenergies are invariant under unit-cell redefinitions, eigenvectors (Bloch states) and derived quantities such as the Zak phase depend on the chosen unit-cell convention. Therefore different physical terminations (different placements of the basis atoms inside the unit cell) yield different Bloch Hamiltonians $h(k)$ whose symmetry properties (for example, the existence or absence of the chiral operator $\Gamma$ satisfying $\Gamma h(k)\Gamma^{-1}=-h(k)$) can differ.

Present the three qualitative boundary behaviors that follow from termination dependence: because termination controls whether the chiral symmetry that quantizes the Zak phase is present, the paper identifies three distinct outcomes for a fixed bulk parameter set: (i) pinned/topological end states when the termination respects the emergent chiral symmetry and thus the multiband Zak phase is quantized, (ii) split/unprotected end states when the termination breaks the protecting chiral symmetry so that in-gap states are not pinned to $E=0$, and (iii) no end states for certain terminations whose local environment and unit-cell choice do not support in-gap localized solutions.
[22]

Provide explicit numerical/constructive evidence by comparing multiple terminations: using four example zigzag terminations (rectangular, modified rectangular, rhombic, modified rhombic) the authors construct their explicit Bloch Hamiltonians (provided in the Appendix) and compute the multiband Zak phase and OBC spectra for odd- and even-width cases. For example, the rectangular and modified rectangular terminations preserve the odd-width chiral symmetry and show quantized Zak phase and pinned end modes, whereas the rhombic termination lacks chiral symmetry and exhibits either no in-gap states or non-quantized Zak phase with non-pinned in-gap states, illustrating the three behaviors above.
Fig. 4(a); Fig. 4(c); Fig. 4(i); Fig. 4(m)

Explain monomode engineering by combining different terminations: by terminating the left and right ends of a finite ribbon with different unit-cell terminations one can arrange that only one end supports a pinned end state while the other does not, thereby realizing a single localized "monomode" end state localized to one termination. This follows from the termination-controlled presence/absence of chiral symmetry locally at each end and is analogous in spirit to termination effects in 1D SSH-like models, though in the nanoribbon the monomode can be switched off by tuning $M$.
[23]

motivating_questions.content: Topological bulk–boundary correspondence relies on matching the bulk unit cell used to compute a topological invariant with the actual finite termination of the system. For honeycomb nanoribbons the unit cell contains multiple atoms, so there is significant freedom in how a ribbon terminates; previous analyses sometimes used a Bloch Hamiltonian corresponding to one termination while drawing OBC conclusions for a different termination. Without a systematic account of how specific terminations map to unit-cell choices and to spectral symmetries (e.g., whether chiral symmetry is present), one cannot predict whether end states are topologically protected, accidental, absent, or manipulable by engineering the termination. This gap prevented controlled proposals for termination-based engineering of end-state spectra and misled earlier comparisons between bulk invariants and OBC spectra.

For staggered 7-AGNR-S(1,m): $m=1$ shows a zero-energy end state ($\mathbb{Z}_{2}=1$), $m=2$ shows a gap closure consistent with $t_{n}\approx t_{m}$, and $m=3$ (the experimentally realised 7-AGNR-S(1,3)) shows a reopened gap with no zero-energy end state, establishing its topologically trivial class ($\mathbb{Z}_{2}=0$). For inline 7-AGNR-I(1,m): LDOS calculations predict a non-trivial to trivial transition between $m=3$ ($\mathbb{Z}_{2}=1$) and $m=4$ ($\mathbb{Z}_{2}=0$); experiment on the backbone-extended 7-AGNR-I(1,3) shows an end-localised spectral feature at approximately $+0.25\ \text{V}$ (shifted from mid-gap by substrate-induced doping and many-body renormalization), consistent with a topologically non-trivial end state and classification $\mathbb{Z}_{2}=1$. Topological phase diagrams over $n\in[1,9]$ and $m\in[1,9]$ are provided (tight-binding).

The staggered structure 7-AGNR-S(1,3) was synthesised on Au(111) by on-surface polymerisation and cyclodehydrogenation of monomer BADMT (monomer 1) and imaged by constant-height nc-AFM. Scanning tunnelling spectroscopy (STS) shows that the pristine 7-AGNR bandgap of $2.4\ \text{eV}$ on Au(111) is reduced to $0.65\pm0.1\ \text{eV}$ in 7-AGNR-S(1,3). Tight-binding modelling of the staggered 7-AGNR-S(1,3) yields an effective cis-SSH dispersion
      $E(k)=\pm\sqrt{t_{n}^{2}+t_{m}^{2}+2t_{n}t_{m}\cos(k)}$
      with fitted coupling parameters $t_{n}=0.45\ \text{eV}$ and $t_{m}=0.59\ \text{eV}$ ($\gamma=2\sqrt{t_{n}^{2}+t_{m}^{2}+2t_{n}t_{m}}$ gives the predicted bandwidth $2.08\ \text{eV}$). steps.reasoning:
Take as established the tight-binding parametrisation that maps edge-extended AGNR families to effective SSH chains with couplings $(t_{n},t_{m})$ (from the tight-binding Hamiltonian with $\gamma_{0}=3\ \text{eV}$) and the experimentally synthesised examples (7-AGNR-S(1,3) and 7-AGNR-I(1,3)) with their fitted couplings; these are the starting points for topological classification via bulk–boundary correspondence. 
Methods

Explain the diagnostic method: since the winding-number topological invariant ($\mathbb{Z}_{2}$) cannot be directly measured experimentally, use the bulk–boundary correspondence which states that a topologically non-trivial bulk ($\mathbb{Z}_{2}=1$) manifests as zero-energy states localised at the chain ends in a finite system, whereas a trivial bulk ($\mathbb{Z}_{2}=0$) lacks such zero-energy end states; thus, compute or measure end-localised LDOS or STS spectra as the practical probe of topological class. 
[11]

Note an important complication and its mitigation: the $N$-AGNR backbone can host zigzag-termini-related end states that are separate in origin from the SSH junction end states and which can hybridise with them, possibly removing or shifting the SSH end-state spectral signature; to prevent this hybridisation, experimentally extend the ribbon terminus by a sufficiently long pristine $N$-AGNR backbone segment so that the SSH end state (if present) is spectroscopically distinguishable. This procedural detail is required for correct application of the bulk–boundary test. 
Fig. 3a

Report tight-binding LDOS results for the staggered family 7-AGNR-S(1,m): for $m=1$ the LDOS at the terminated end exhibits a zero-energy end state, consistent with a non-trivial topological phase ($\mathbb{Z}_{2}=1$) and the condition $t_{n}<t_{m}$; increasing $m$ reduces $t_{m}$, and for $m=2$ the LDOS shows a gap closure consistent with $t_{n}\approx t_{m}$ (the metallic transition), whereas for $m=3$ the gap reopens and no zero-energy end state is present, indicating that 7-AGNR-S(1,3) is topologically trivial ($\mathbb{Z}_{2}=0$) according to the tight-binding LDOS calculations. 
Fig. 3a

Report experimental verification for the staggered 7-AGNR-S(1,3): after synthesising a ribbon with a pristine 7-AGNR backbone extension to avoid zigzag end-state hybridisation, differential-conductance ($dI/dV$) spectra and spatial $dI/dV$ maps measured at the chain end show no zero-energy end state and instead show features corresponding to the valence-band onset at $-0.05\ \text{V}$ and conduction-band onset at $+0.65\ \text{V}$ with a featureless gap at $+0.25\ \text{V}$, in agreement with the tight-binding charge-density simulations; this experimental observation confirms the tight-binding prediction that 7-AGNR-S(1,3) is topologically trivial ($\mathbb{Z}_{2}=0$). 
Fig. 3e
Fig. 3f

Report tight-binding LDOS results for the inline family 7-AGNR-I(1,m): the LDOS series evaluated at the end of the 7-AGNR-I(1,m) segment predicts a topological transition between $m=3$ and $m=4$, with $m=3$ showing zero-energy end states (topologically non-trivial, $\mathbb{Z}_{2}=1$) and $m=4$ exhibiting a nearly closed gap with disappearance of zero-energy states (topologically trivial, $\mathbb{Z}_{2}=0$); thus TB predicts a non-trivial-to-trivial transition at $m=4$ for the inline family. 
Fig. 4b

Provide experimental evidence for the inline 7-AGNR-I(1,3): nc-AFM imaging verifies the structural model; $dI/dV$ spectra recorded at the chain end show a state at approximately $+0.25\ \text{V}$ that is localised at the ribbon end in $dI/dV$ mapping; comparison with tight-binding simulations assigns the $+0.25\ \text{V}$ spectral feature to the expected topological end state, noting that the state appears at $+0.25\ \text{V}$ rather than exactly $0\ \text{V}$ because of substrate-induced charge doping on Au(111) and possible many-body energy renormalization effects. These experimental observations support the classification of 7-AGNR-I(1,3) as topologically non-trivial ($\mathbb{Z}_{2}=1$). 
Fig. 4d
[29]

Conclude that combining tight-binding LDOS calculations (bulk) with end-terminated experimental STS (boundary) maps the topological phase transitions in the $(n,m)$ parameter space for both staggered 7-AGNR-S$(n,m)$ and inline 7-AGNR-I$(n,m)$ families via bulk–boundary correspondence, and that topological phase diagrams over $n\in[1,9]$ and $m\in[1,9]$ were generated by tight-binding calculations to summarise these transitions.

motivating_questions.content: Establishing the topological class of an engineered one-dimensional band structure in a real solid-state ribbon requires an experimental protocol robust to competing and substrate-related end/edge states. The winding number cannot be measured directly; instead, the bulk–boundary correspondence is used, but in AGNR-derived systems zigzag-related end states and substrate effects can hybridize with SSH-type modes and shift them away from zero energy. What was needed was (i) tight-binding predictions showing where zero-energy end states should occur across $(n,m)$, (ii) synthesis of ribbon segments with controlled end extensions to suppress hybridization from backbone zigzag end states, and (iii) STS/LDOS measurements that confirm the presence or absence of end-localised states in agreement with the predicted phase boundaries. Prior to this work no such combined theoretical–synthetic–spectroscopic mapping had been demonstrated for AGNR-based SSH analogues.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: The $R|P^{3}$ tight-binding model exhibits both intrinsic, termination-independent symmetry-protected topological phases (SPTPs) and extrinsic, termination-dependent boundary-obstructed topological phases (BOTPs). Concretely, the bulk octupole moment (quantized nested polarization $=1/2$) produces intrinsic SPTPs in the parameter region $|\eta|<1$, while suitable changes to hopping strengths along directions with open or periodic boundary conditions can induce surface or hinge gap closures that produce boundary-localized transitions (surface-obstructed and hinge-obstructed transitions) without necessarily closing the bulk gap; these termination-dependent transitions alter edge polarization and can remove surface/hinge modes even when the bulk invariant remains nontrivial.

premises.content:
A concrete eight-band tight-binding Hamiltonian defined on the momentum-space $R|P^{3}$ lattice that is constrained by the k-NS symmetries and chiral symmetry is given (for isotropic intra-cell coupling $ \gamma $ and inter-cell coupling $ \lambda $) by
      \[
      \begin{aligned}
      H(k_x,k_y,k_z)=&\;\lambda\big(-\cos k_x\,\Gamma'_3-\sin k_x\,\Gamma'_0+\cos k_y\,\Gamma'_1\\
      &-\sin k_y\,\Gamma'_2-\cos k_z\,\Gamma'_0+\sin k_z\,\Gamma'_5\big)+\gamma\cdot\zeta,
      \end{aligned}
      \]
      where the $8\times8$ matrices are defined as $ \Gamma'_0=\sigma_1\otimes\Gamma_0 $, $ \Gamma'_i=\sigma_0\otimes\Gamma_i $ $(i=1,2,3,4)$, $ \Gamma'_5=\sigma_2\otimes\Gamma_0 $, with $ \Gamma_0=\sigma_3\otimes\tau_0 $, $ \Gamma_j=\sigma_1\otimes\tau_j $ $(j=1,2,3)$, $ \Gamma_4=\sigma_2\otimes\tau_0 $, and
      $$\zeta=\sigma_3\tau_1 s_0+\sigma_1\tau_0 s_0-\sigma_3\tau_2 s_2.$$
      Here $ \sigma_\alpha $, $ \tau_\beta $, and $ s_\gamma $ denote Pauli matrices acting on sublattice/site degrees of freedom along the $x$, $y$, and $z$ directions, respectively. This Hamiltonian respects the three k-NS reflection operators $\mathcal{M}_x:(k_x,k_y,k_z)\rightarrow(-k_x,k_y+\pi,k_z+\pi)$, $\mathcal{M}_y:(k_x,k_y,k_z)\rightarrow(k_x+\pi,-k_y,k_z+\pi)$, $\mathcal{M}_z:(k_x,k_y,k_z)\rightarrow(k_x+\pi,k_y+\pi,-k_z)$, the pairwise inversion products $\mathcal{P}_{xy}=\mathcal{M}_x\mathcal{M}_y$, $\mathcal{P}_{yz}=\mathcal{M}_y\mathcal{M}_z$, $\mathcal{P}_{xz}=\mathcal{M}_x\mathcal{M}_z$, ordinary inversion $I=\mathcal{M}_x\mathcal{M}_y\mathcal{M}_z$, and a chiral symmetry $ \mathcal{C} $ with $ \mathcal{C}H\mathcal{C}^\dagger=-H $.

steps.reasoning: Start from the tight-binding Hamiltonian constrained by k-NS and chiral symmetries (conclusion 2) and from the nested-polarization topological classification (conclusion 3) that identifies the octupole topological regime as $|\eta|<1$ with nested polarization $=1/2$.

Characterize intrinsic symmetry-protected topological phases (SPTPs): assert that the bulk octupole moment, quantified by the nested polarization $=1/2$ in the parameter region $|\eta|<1$, constitutes an intrinsic, termination-independent SPTP because it arises from bulk band-structure topology (i.e., a bulk topological invariant) and is robust to boundary termination so long as the bulk gap remains open.
Fig. 2(d)

Describe extrinsic, boundary-obstructed topological phases (BOTPs): explain that suitable modifications to hopping strengths (i.e., tuning of $\gamma$ and/or $\lambda$ anisotropically or along directions with chosen boundary conditions) can close and reopen gaps localized at surfaces or hinges while leaving the bulk gap intact, thereby producing boundary-localized transitions (surface-obstructed and hinge-obstructed transitions) that depend on the boundary termination; these are extrinsic because they alter boundary spectra without requiring a bulk gap closure.
Fig. 3(a–f)

Provide the concrete scenarios the authors present: (a) in the semi-open case with open boundary conditions (OBCs) in $x$ and periodic boundary conditions (PBCs) in $y$ and $z$, tuning the hopping parameters across $|\eta_y|=|\eta_z|=1$ can close a surface gap and remove surface states (i.e., a surface-obstructed transition) as the system moves between colored regions of the phase diagram; (b) in the semi-open case with OBCs in $x$ and $y$ and PBC in $z$, varying $\eta_z$ across $|\eta_z|=1$ can close surface/hinge gaps and remove hinge states (i.e., a hinge-obstructed transition); both cases change edge polarization and boundary modes while potentially leaving the bulk invariant unchanged.
Fig. 3(a–f)

Conclude the coexistence statement: combine the intrinsic SPTP statement (bulk octupole invariant $=1/2$ for $|\eta|<1$) and the extrinsic BOTP behavior (boundary-gap closures and edge-polarization changes induced by boundary-termination-dependent hopping variations) to assert that the $R|P^{3}$ tight-binding model exhibits both intrinsic (termination-independent) SPTPs and extrinsic (termination-dependent) BOTPs, and that boundary-obstructed transitions can remove surface/hinge modes even when the bulk topological invariant remains nontrivial.

motivating_questions.content: In higher-order topology it matters whether boundary-localized modes are enforced by a bulk topological invariant (intrinsic SPTPs) or arise from boundary obstructions that depend on termination (extrinsic BOTPs). Prior examples typically addressed one class or the other, but there was no three-dimensional model on a projective Brillouin manifold demonstrating both phenomena and clarifying how k-NS symmetries constrain which boundary transitions are intrinsic versus termination-induced. Without such an example it remained unclear how projective-space symmetries enable surface- or hinge-obstructed transitions coexisting with a bulk octupole invariant and how parameter variation under different boundary conditions maps to surface/hinge/bulk gap closures.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: Independent calculations show that monolayer $1T'$-WTe$_2$ hosts topological edge states arising from the nontrivial topology of the bulk bands: (a) a tight-binding model constructed from the bulk electronic structure, analyzed with the iterative surface Green's function method, reveals edge-localized bands that traverse the bulk gap region; (b) topological invariants computed using both the n-field approach and the hybrid Wannier charge-center (Wilson loop) method confirm a nontrivial $Z_2$ topology for the monolayer, implying topologically protected helical edge modes; and (c) these topological edge modes are found in calculations for different edge terminations (both $a$- and $b$-direction terminations) and persist when edge potential and structural relaxations are included in ab initio ribbon calculations. The calculations therefore establish that edge-localized states of topological origin are an intrinsic property of monolayer $1T'$-WTe$_2$ and are not removed by reasonable changes in edge termination or local relaxation.

A practical, computationally efficient algorithm to evaluate the Hopf invariant $n_h$ for any two-band, gapped band Hamiltonian defined on the Brillouin-zone torus $T^{3}$ is provided: starting from the normalized three-component vector $\hat{\boldsymbol{n}}(\boldsymbol{k})$ that parametrizes the two-band Hamiltonian $H(\boldsymbol{k})=\hat{\boldsymbol{n}}(\boldsymbol{k})\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}$, compute the local current density
      $j_{\mu}(\boldsymbol{k})=\frac{1}{8\pi}\epsilon_{\mu\nu\lambda}\,\hat{\boldsymbol{n}}\cdot(\partial_{\nu}\hat{\boldsymbol{n}}\times\partial_{\lambda}\hat{\boldsymbol{n}})$ on a discrete grid of $N$ points in the Brillouin zone, Fourier-transform $j(\boldsymbol{k})$ to momentum space, solve the magnetostatic equation $\nabla\times \boldsymbol{A} = \boldsymbol{j}$ in the discrete momentum-space Coulomb gauge $\partial_{\mu}A_{\mu}=0$ (by algebraic inversion in Fourier components), and evaluate the Hopf invariant by the discrete integral
      $n_{h}=-\int_{T^{3}} d^{3}k\; \boldsymbol{j}(\boldsymbol{k})\cdot\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{k})$.
      Implemented on an $N$-point grid this procedure requires $O(N\log N)$ time due to the use of fast Fourier transforms, and yields integer-valued invariants that converge with grid refinement.

A two-dimensional tight-binding Bogoliubov–de Gennes Hamiltonian on the eightfold symmetric Ammann–Beenker tiling is given by 
      $$
      \mathcal{H}=\sum_j\boldsymbol{\Psi}_j^\dagger\mathcal{H}_j\boldsymbol{\Psi}_j+\sum_{\langle j,k\rangle}\boldsymbol{\Psi}_j^\dagger\mathcal{H}_{jk}\boldsymbol{\Psi}_k,
      $$
      with local Nambu spinor $\boldsymbol{\Psi}_j^\dagger=(\psi_{j,\uparrow}^{\dagger},\psi_{j,\uparrow},\psi_{j,\downarrow}^{\dagger},\psi_{j,\downarrow})$, on-site term 
      $$
      \mathcal{H}_j=\mu\,\sigma_z\tau_z,
      $$
      where $\mu$ is the chemical potential, $\sigma_a$ and $\tau_a$ ($a=x,y,z$) are Pauli matrices acting on spin and particle-hole degrees of freedom, respectively, and $\sigma_0$ and $\tau_0$ are identity matrices in those spaces. The nearest-neighbor hopping and $p$-wave pairing are 
      $$
      \mathcal{H}_{jk}=\frac{t}{2}\sigma_z\tau_z+\frac{\Delta}{2i}\big[\cos(\alpha_{jk})\sigma_z\tau_x+\sin(\alpha_{jk})\sigma_z\tau_y\big],
      $$
      where $t$ is the hopping strength, $\Delta$ is the pairing strength, and $\alpha_{jk}$ is the angle of the bond from site $j$ to $k$. Introducing the symmetry-breaking perturbation 
      $$
      \mathcal{V}=\sum_{\langle j,k\rangle}\boldsymbol{\Psi}_j^\dagger\mathcal{V}_{jk}\boldsymbol{\Psi}_k,\qquad
      \mathcal{V}_{jk}=\frac{V}{2}\sigma_y\tau_0\cos(4\alpha_{jk}),
      $$

premises.content:
A three-band tight-binding Hamiltonian for spinless fermionic atoms trapped on a honeycomb-like optical lattice with three inequivalent sublattice sites A, B, C is defined by the second-quantized operator
      $$
      \hat{H}=\hat{H}_T+\hat{H}_L+\hat{H}_V,
      $$
      with
      $$
      \begin{aligned}
      \hat{H}_T & = -t\sum_{\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle}\big(\hat{a}_i^\dagger\hat{a}_j+\hat{b}_i^\dagger\hat{b}_j+\hat{c}_i^\dagger\hat{c}_j\big),\\
      \hat{H}_L & = \lambda_a\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\hat{c}_i^\dagger\hat{a}_j e^{i\phi_{ij}}+\lambda_b\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\hat{c}_i^\dagger\hat{b}_j e^{i\phi_{ij}} + \mathrm{h.c.},\\
      \hat{H}_V & = \Delta_a\sum_j\hat{a}_j^\dagger\hat{a}_j + \Delta_b\sum_j\hat{b}_j^\dagger\hat{b}_j.
      \end{aligned}
      $$
      In these expressions $\hat{a}_i,\hat{b}_i,\hat{c}_i$ annihilate a fermion on lattice site $i$ of sublattices A, B, C respectively; $t\in\mathbb{R}$ is the normal next-nearest-neighbour (NNN) hopping amplitude within each triangular sublattice (sum over $\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle$); $\lambda_a,\lambda_b\in\mathbb{C}$ are laser-assisted nearest-neighbour (NN) tunneling amplitudes (sums over NN pairs $\langle i,j\rangle$) accompanied by Peierls phases $\phi_{ij}=\mathbf{p}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_i+\mathbf{r}_j)/2$ where $\mathbf{p}$ is the Raman recoil momentum imparted by the laser beams and $\mathbf{r}_i$ is the position of site $i$; and $\Delta_a,\Delta_b$ are on-site resonance detunings that act as effective sublattice potentials. Performing the unitary gauge transformation
      $$
      \hat{a}_j\to\hat{a}_j e^{-i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{r}_j/2},\quad \hat{b}_j\to\hat{b}_j e^{-i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{r}_j/2},\quad \hat{c}_j\to\hat{c}_j e^{i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{r}_j/2}
      $$
      removes the explicit spatial dependence of the NN Peierls factors and yields real NN tunneling together with complex NNN tunneling phases parametrized by staggered flux angles $\phi_i=\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{u}_i/2$, where $\mathbf{u}_i$ ($i=1,2,3$) denote the three NNN displacement vectors. In momentum space, with the spinor $\hat{\Psi}_k=(\hat{a}_k,\hat{c}_k,\hat{b}_k)^T$, the Bloch Hamiltonian takes the $3\times3$ form
      $$
      \hat{H}_k=\begin{pmatrix}
      \xi_a^k & (\lambda_a^k)^* & 0\\
      \lambda_a^k & \xi_c^k & (\lambda_b^k)^*\\
      0 & \lambda_b^k & \xi_b^k
      \end{pmatrix},
      $$
      with
      $$
      \begin{aligned}
      \xi_{a(b)}^{k} &= \Delta_{a(b)} - 2t\sum_{i=1}^3\cos(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{u}_i+\phi_i),\\
      \xi_c^k &= -2t\sum_{i=1}^3\cos(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{u}_i-\phi_i),\\
      \lambda_{a(b)}^k &= \lambda_{a(b)}\sum_{i=1}^3 e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\nu_i},
      \end{aligned}
      $$
      where $\nu_i$ ($i=1,2,3$) are the three NN displacement vectors. The microscopic ingredients required for experimental realization are therefore: three internal atomic states localized on inequivalent sublattice sites A, B, C; Raman-assisted NN tunneling amplitudes $\lambda_{a},\lambda_{b}$ with recoil momentum $\mathbf{p}$ producing Peierls phases; normal NNN hopping $t$ within each triangular sublattice; and on-site detunings $\Delta_{a},\Delta_{b}$. The Hamiltonian (above) yields three Bloch bands whose band topology depends on the staggered fluxes $\phi_i$, the detunings $\Delta_{a,b}$ and the tunneling amplitudes $t,\lambda_{a,b}$.

premises.content:
For the three-band Bloch Hamiltonian defined above, the Chern number $C_n$ of band $n$ equals one over $2\pi$ times the sum of the Berry-phase contributions from small contours encircling the two inequivalent Dirac points $K$ and $K'$ in the Brillouin zone:
      $$
      C_n=\frac{1}{2\pi}\big(\gamma_K+\gamma_{K'}\big),
      $$
      where the local Berry-phase contribution at a Dirac point is $\gamma=-\int_0^{2\pi}d\theta\;\langle\psi|\,i\partial_\theta\,|\psi\rangle$ with $\psi$ the normalized Bloch eigenvector expressed in polar coordinates $q=(|q|,\theta_q)$ about the Dirac point. The two inequivalent Dirac-point momenta are
      $$
      K=\Big(\frac{4\pi}{3\sqrt{3}},\,0\Big),\qquad K'=\Big(-\frac{4\pi}{3\sqrt{3}},\,0\Big).
      $$
      Near these Dirac points the normalized eigenvectors for the three bands, labeled here by the sublattice index that dominates the weight, have the asymptotic angular dependence (with $\theta_q$ the azimuthal angle of the small momentum $q$ measured from the Dirac point)
      $$
      \begin{aligned}
      \psi_{a,q} &= (1,0,0)^T,\quad \psi_{a,q'}=(1,0,0)^T,\\
      \psi_{b,q} &= (0,0,e^{-i2\theta_q})^T,\quad \psi_{b,q'}=(0,0,e^{i2\theta_q})^T,\\
      \psi_{c,q} &= (0,e^{-i\theta_q},0)^T,\quad \psi_{c,q'}=(0,e^{i\theta_q},0)^T.
      \end{aligned}
      $$
      Evaluating the contour integral for each of these asymptotic angular eigenvectors gives quantized contributions $\gamma\in\{0,4\pi,\mp2\pi\}$ at a Dirac point, so that $C_n$ is an integer equal to the sum of the two Dirac-point contributions divided by $2\pi$. Consequently, the Chern number of a band can be determined operationally from the ordering (relative energy positions) of the band energies $E_n(k)$ evaluated at $K$ and $K'$ because the singular behaviour of the Bloch eigenvectors at those two points controls the nonzero Berry-phase contributions.

A four-band tight-binding model on the honeycomb lattice with two internal (pseudospin) states per lattice site is defined in momentum space by the $4\times4$ Bloch Hamiltonian in the basis $\Psi_k=(\hat{a}_{k\uparrow},\hat{a}_{k\downarrow},\hat{b}_{k\uparrow},\hat{b}_{k\downarrow})^T$,
      $$
      \hat{H}_k=\begin{pmatrix}
      t_k^a-\delta+\varepsilon & d & 0 & \lambda_k\\
      d & t_k^a-\delta-\varepsilon & \lambda_k & 0\\
      0 & \lambda_k^* & t_k^b+\delta+\varepsilon & d\\
      \lambda_k^* & 0 & d & t_k^b+\delta-\varepsilon
      \end{pmatrix},
      $$
      where $t_k^{a,b}=-2t_{a,b}\sum_{i=1}^3\cos(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{u}_i\pm\phi_i)$ are the sublattice-dependent NNN dispersions (with $\phi_i=\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{u}_i/2$), $\lambda_k=\lambda\sum_{i=1}^3 e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\nu_i}$ is the Raman-assisted NN form factor, $\varepsilon$ is half the internal-state energy splitting, $d$ is an on-site dipole-coupling-induced $\sigma_x$ term coupling the internal states, and $\delta$ is the staggered sublattice resonance detuning. Defining $t_k^{0,1}=(t_k^a\pm t_k^b)/2$, the four band energies are given in closed form by
      $$
      E_k = t_k^0 \pm \sqrt{d^2+\varepsilon^2+|\lambda_k|^2+(t_k^1-\delta)^2\pm 2\sqrt{(d^2+\varepsilon^2)(t_k^1-\delta)^2+d^2|\lambda_k|^2}}.
      $$
      The two middle bands touch at the Dirac points $K,K'$ when the condition
      $$
      (t_k^1-\delta)^2=\varepsilon^2+d^2
      $$
      holds at those momenta; consequently, for a half-filled system the ground state is topologically nontrivial when the staggered detuning $\delta$ lies inside either of the intervals
      $$
      \delta\in\big(t_K^1\pm\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+d^2},\; t_{K'}^1\pm\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+d^2}\big),
      $$
      with Chern number magnitude $|C|=1$ when $\delta$ lies in one such interval and $|C|=2$ when $\delta$ lies in the overlap of the two intervals, corresponding respectively to one or two pairs of chiral edge modes.

Describe the bulk Berry-phase calculation: define the Berry phase $\gamma(C)$ as the gauge-invariant phase obtained by integrating the Berry connection around a closed loop $C$ in 2D momentum space; the authors numerically evaluate the Berry phase for a closed loop encircling a single bulk BCP in FeB$_2$ (i.e., choose a small loop in $k$-space around one crossing point and sum the Berry connection for the occupied band(s) along that loop). motivating_questions.content: Establishing that an enforced BCP is not merely a symmetry-degeneracy but also carries a nontrivial topological invariant is crucial for predicting robust boundary phenomena (edge states) and for connecting bulk band topology to observable surface modes. The Berry-phase calculation and the ribbon-state analysis bridge the bulk symmetry-enforcement picture and experimentally measurable edge-state phenomenology, thus providing concrete predictions for spectroscopic edge probes (ARPES, STM) and transport measurements on ribbons or finite flakes.

premises.content:
A concrete four-band tight-binding Hamiltonian on the diamond lattice is introduced that realizes the different three-dimensional topological classes:
      $$
      H = t\sum_{\langle ij\rangle} c_i^\dagger c_j + i\left(\frac{8\lambda_{\mathrm{SO}}}{a^2}\right)\sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle} c_i^\dagger\,\mathbf{s}\cdot\bigl(\mathbf{d}_{ij}^1\times\mathbf{d}_{ij}^2\bigr)\,c_j,
      $$
      where the first sum is over nearest neighbors with hopping amplitude $t$, the second sum is over second-neighbor pairs with spin Pauli matrices $\mathbf{s}$, $\mathbf{d}_{ij}^{1,2}$ are the two nearest-neighbor bond vectors forming the two-step path between the second neighbors, $a$ is the cubic cell size, and $\lambda_{\mathrm{SO}}$ parameterizes the spin-orbit coupling. In this model the conduction and valence bands touch at three inequivalent $X$ points $X^{r}=2\pi\hat{r}/a$, and small symmetry-lowering perturbations of the four nearest-neighbor bonds $t\to t+\delta t_p$ open gaps. Near $X^{z}$ the low-energy effective Hamiltonian is a $3+1$-dimensional Dirac model
      $$
      \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{z}=t a\,\sigma^{y} q_{z} + 4\lambda_{\mathrm{SO}} a\,\sigma^{z}\bigl(s^{x}q_{x}-s^{y}q_{y}\bigr) + m^{z}\sigma^{x},
      $$
      with $\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{k}-X^{z}$, sublattice Pauli matrices $\sigma^{i}$, spin Pauli matrices $s^{i}$, and mass $m^{z}=\sum_p\delta t_p\,\mathrm{sgn}[\mathbf{d}_p\cdot\hat{z}]$. Analogous Dirac forms apply near $X^{x,y}$ by permutation of coordinates. Tuning the signs of these masses across $X^{r}$ drives transitions between distinct topological phases in this lattice model.

premises.content:
For the diamond-lattice tight-binding model with nearest-neighbor bond modulations $t\rightarrow t+\delta t_p$, the time-reversal-invariant momentum (TRIM) sign $\delta_i$ can be determined analytically by
      $$
      \delta_{i}=\operatorname{sgn}\Biggl[\sum_{p}\bigl(t+\delta t_{p}\bigr)\cos\bigl(\Gamma_{i}\cdot(\mathbf{d}_{p}-\mathbf{d}_{1})\bigr)\Biggr],
      $$
      where the sum runs over the four nearest-neighbor bond vectors $\mathbf{d}_p$ and $\Gamma_i$ are the eight bulk TRIM. In particular, for small $\delta t_p$ one finds a specific pattern with $\delta=+1$ at $\mathbf{k}=0$ and three $L$ points and $\delta=-1$ at the remaining $L$ point, while at each $X^{r}$ one has $\delta=\mathrm{sgn}[m^{r}]$ with $m^{r}$ the Dirac mass at $X^{r}$. Using this formula the model parameter regimes are identified: when one nearest-neighbor bond is weaker than the others ($\delta t_p<0$ for a single $p$) the system is in a weak topological insulator (WTI) phase corresponding to quantum spin Hall (QSH) layers stacked along $\mathbf{d}_p$, whereas if one bond is stronger the system is in one of four strong topological insulator (STI) phases; a trivial band insulator (with all four $Z_2$ invariants zero, $0;(000)$) occurs in this model when, for example, $\delta t_1>2t$ (or when a sufficiently strong staggered sublattice potential is applied).

premises.content: A practical numerical workflow for evaluating the real-space Euler formula and local marker is specified. First, diagonalize the finite-system Hamiltonian to obtain eigenvectors and construct the projector $P=\Pi\,\mathbf{1}_{\mathrm{occ}}\,\Pi^{-1}$ in a local orbital basis (with $\Pi$ matrix of eigenvectors and $\mathbf{1}_{\mathrm{occ}}$ the projector onto occupied eigenstates in the eigenbasis). Second, construct composite Wannier functions via a unitary transformation $S$ (obtained by minimizing the Marzari–Vanderbilt localization functional) to separate coordinate and internal subspaces so that the occupied internal submatrix is well-defined and ordered. Third, compute the matrix $M=S\Pi^{-1}\,P\,[U P U^\dagger,V P V^\dagger]\,\Pi S^{-1}$, where $U$ and $V$ are the matrix representations of the unitary position operators $\hat{U}=\exp(2\pi\mathrm{i}\hat{X}/L_x)$ and $\hat{V}=\exp(2\pi\mathrm{i}\hat{Y}/L_y)$ in the local basis. Perform the trace over coordinate indices and take the Pfaffian over the occupied internal block to obtain the local marker $e(\boldsymbol{r})$ via $e(\boldsymbol{r}) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \operatorname{Pf}_{\mathrm{occ}}(\langle\boldsymbol{r}| \hat{P}[\hat{U}\hat{P}\hat{U}^\dagger, \hat{V}\hat{P}\hat{V}^\dagger] |\boldsymbol{r}\rangle)$ and the global Euler number $e$ via $e = \frac{1}{2\pi} \operatorname{Tr} \operatorname{Pf}_{\mathrm{occ}}(\hat{P}[\hat{U}\hat{P}\hat{U}^\dagger, \hat{V}\hat{P}\hat{V}^\dagger])$. The implementation requires using the unitary position operators $\hat{U},\hat{V}$ (not their first-order Taylor expansions $\hat{X},\hat{Y}$) to preserve real-valuedness under $\mathscr{P}\mathscr{T}$ (space-time inversion) symmetry constraints.

premises.content: The chiral (sublattice) symmetry relied upon in many tight-binding toy models to protect zero-energy boundary states requires exact conditions — strictly equal on-site energies (often set to zero) and the absence of certain (e.g., next-nearest-neighbor) hoppings — that are not generically satisfied in real quantum materials. Real quantum Hamiltonians have spectra bounded below but not above, so strict particle-hole symmetric spectral placement about zero is not a generic physical symmetry; differences between on-site potentials at sample orbitals and vacuum sites at boundaries break the model chiral symmetry in any realistic embedding. Experimental classical simulators that are used to emulate these quantum systems show spectral asymmetry (lack of mid-gap spectral mirror symmetry), indicating that the chiral symmetry is not exact in those realizations. Therefore, the symmetry protection mechanism that would salvage boundary robustness even if Berry diagnostics were ambiguous is not present in realistic systems, and observed corner states in experiments are not protected by an exact chiral symmetry.

State the logical synthesis: because (i) Berry/Wannier diagnostics are unit-cell-dependent and hence do not uniquely classify the bulk, (ii) the same bulk Hamiltonian can be assigned either the "topological" or "trivial" label by changing unit-cell bookkeeping, and (iii) boundary-localized modes can be created or destroyed by altering the boundary termination even when symmetries are preserved, the conventional dichotomy "topological vs trivial" assigned by those diagnostics does not correspond to an intrinsic bulk phase distinction for the class of tight-binding models considered.

Incorporate the absence of realistic symmetry protection: since the chiral (sublattice) symmetry that might be invoked to salvage robustness of zero-energy boundary modes is not physically realizable in generic quantum systems and is typically absent in experimental implementations, the possibility of rescuing a bulk-phase interpretation of the boundary phenomenology via exact symmetry protection is not available in realistic settings; thus the boundary distinctions cannot be elevated to bona fide bulk phase distinctions by appealing to chiral protection.

Conclude explicitly that for the class of tight-binding models and examples examined in the paper, whenever the bulk is gapped the system corresponds to a single bulk phase: the labels "topological" and "trivial" assigned by unit-cell-dependent Berry/Wannier diagnostics do not indicate distinct bulk phases, and any differences in boundary spectra (presence or absence of corner states) are attributable to boundary/termination choices or to unit-cell bookkeeping rather than to an intrinsic bulk phase transition.

motivating_questions.content: A central aim of topological band theory is to establish robust distinctions between qualitatively different bulk phases that have observable consequences (e.g., protected boundary modes). If putative invariants are ambiguous and boundary spectra can be altered without changing the bulk Hamiltonian, then the identification of distinct bulk phases becomes ill-posed. Prior literature had reported pairs of phases (topological vs trivial) for several lattice models based on Berry-phase diagnostics and corresponding boundary phenomena; this raises the question whether those phase distinctions survive a requirement of bulk-uniqueness of invariants and boundary-independence of classification. If they do not, then the purported multiplicity of bulk phases for these models collapses to a single gapped bulk phase and the emphasis must shift to boundary engineering rather than bulk topology.

Energy spectra were computed as functions of $k_{\parallel}$ for representative ribbon terminations (W-terminated $x$-ribbon, Te-terminated $x$-ribbon, straight $y$-termination, and sawtooth $y$-termination), where each termination corresponds to a different truncation of the bulk lattice and hence different atomic edge configurations; the spectra were plotted close to the Fermi level to examine edge bands relative to the bulk gap.

All ribbons show two pairs of isolated bands corresponding to counterpropagating helical edge states that traverse the bulk energy gap and which are spatially localized to opposite edges of the ribbon; this is the generic hallmark of a $Z_{2}=1$ quantum spin Hall insulator and is independent of termination.

Despite their universal existence, the detailed dispersion of the edge bands depends qualitatively on the atomic termination: in the W-terminated $x$-ribbon the edge bands do not cross each other in the energy window shown and no Kramers crossing at $k_{\parallel}=0$ is observed inside the plotted window; in the Te-terminated $x$-ribbon the edge bands cross at the time-reversal invariant edge momentum $k_{\parallel}=k_{x}=0$ but this crossing (a Kramers doublet or Dirac point) lies energetically far outside the bulk energy gap (i.e., buried in the bulk bands); similarly the straight $y$-termination has an edge Dirac point at $k_{\parallel}=k_{y}=\pi/b$ lying energetically far below the bulk gap.

The sawtooth $y$-termination differs qualitatively: its edge bands cross at the time-reversal invariant edge momentum $k_{\parallel}=k_{y}=0$ and this crossing lies energetically inside the bulk energy gap, i.e., the sawtooth $y$-ribbon realizes an in-gap edge Dirac point.

      $$
      h_{\text{cp}}(t,t')=\begin{pmatrix}
      E_0 & t & 0 & t' \\
      t & E_0 & t & 0 \\
      0 & t & E_0 & t \\
      t' & 0 & t & E_0
      \end{pmatrix}
      $$
      with $E_0=0$, and the coupling between adjacent unit cells is given by the $4\times4$ inter-cell matrix
      $$
      C(t,t')=\begin{pmatrix}
      0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
      0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
      0 & t' & 0 & 0 \\
      t & 0 & 0 & 0
      \end{pmatrix},
      $$

These edge states persist for both $t'/t < 1$ and $t'/t > 1$ parameter regimes, appearing at energies near zero, separated from bulk bands, demonstrating bulk–boundary correspondence for the twofold topological transition.

The Berry phase for band index $s$ is $\beta_s=s\pi w$, so the two phases carry opposite Berry-phase signs.

steps.reasoning:
Construct the finite-chain tight-binding Hamiltonian using the four-site unit-cell block matrices: define the intra-cell (cell-period) block matrix $h_{\text{cp}}(t,t')$ by
$$
h_{\text{cp}}(t,t')=\begin{pmatrix}
E_0 & t & 0 & t' \\
t & E_0 & t & 0 \\
0 & t & E_0 & t \\
t' & 0 & t & E_0
\end{pmatrix},
$$
where $E_0$ is the site energy, $t$ is the first-neighbor hopping, and $t'$ is the third-neighbor hopping; and define the inter-cell coupling block $C(t,t')$ by
$$
C(t,t')=\begin{pmatrix}
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & t' & 0 & 0 \\
t & 0 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix},
$$
so that the finite-chain Hamiltonian for $N$ repeated unit cells acquires a block-Toeplitz form.

Assemble the full finite-chain Hamiltonian for $N$ unit cells in block matrix form (Toeplitz structure): the Hamiltonian $H_{\text{fc}}(t,t')$ is the $4N\times4N$ matrix with $h_{\text{cp}}(t,t')$ on the diagonal and $C(t,t')$ (and its Hermitian conjugate $C^\dagger(t,t')$) on the off-diagonals, explicitly
$$
H_{\text{fc}}(t,t')=
\begin{pmatrix}
h_{\text{cp}} & C & 0 & \dots & 0 \\
C^\dagger & h_{\text{cp}} & C & 0 & \dots \\
0 & C^\dagger & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\vdots &  & \ddots & h_{\text{cp}} & C \\
0 & \dots & 0 & C^\dagger & h_{\text{cp}}
\end{pmatrix},
$$
with all blocks depending parametrically on $t$ and $t'$ and $E_0$.

Diagonalize the finite-chain Hamiltonian numerically for a representative large-$N$ system to probe edge physics; the authors take $N=30$ unit cells (thus a $120\times120$ matrix) and compute the spectrum as a function of the hopping ratio $t'/t$, producing band plots where turquoise curves indicate bulk bands and red curves highlight midgap edge bands.
Fig. 2

Identify in-gap eigenstates and analyze their spatial profiles: the authors report eigenstates whose eigenvalues lie inside the bulk gap and whose eigenfunctions (plotted as amplitude versus site index $j$) are exponentially localized at the chain ends, with amplitude decaying exponentially into the bulk; examples shown include states at energy $E=0$ for $t'/t=0.5$ and for $t'/t=2$, both displaying edge localization, whereas bulk states (e.g., at $E=0.95t$ and $t'/t=2$) have extended profiles across the chain.
Fig. 2

Establish robustness across topological regimes: the edge-localized in-gap states persist for parameter regimes corresponding to both bulk winding numbers found in the infinite system (both for $t'/t<1$ and for $t'/t>1$), and they appear at energies separated from the bulk bands (for example near $E=0$ in the computed examples), thereby demonstrating the bulk–boundary correspondence associated with the twofold topological transition.

motivating_questions.content: Bulk topological invariants predict edge-localized modes only insofar as a finite-size realization respects the assumptions of the bulk model (boundary termination, absence of symmetry-breaking perturbations). Prior to computing finite-chain spectra for the four-site unit-cell model with first- and third-neighbor hoppings, it was not known whether the twofold bulk topology (opposite winding numbers for different $t'$ regimes) actually produces spatially localized, robust edge modes in realistic finite lattices, nor whether those modes persist when $t'$ is varied across the predicted transition. Demonstrating localized edge eigenstates in a finite Hamiltonian with explicit inter-cell coupling blocks and verifying their exponential localization is necessary to establish that the predicted bulk topology has the expected observable boundary signatures.

premises.content:
A general mapping reduces a two-dimensional lattice Bogoliubov–de Gennes (BdG) model, with a periodic chain of scalar impurities described by $H_{\mathrm{imp}}=\hat{U}\sum_n \delta_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}_n}$ where $\mathbf{r}_n=n a_0\mathbf{e}_x$, to an effective one-dimensional supercell Hamiltonian for the impurity bands,
      $$
      H_{\mathrm{eff}}(k_x)=\hat{U}^{-1}\tilde{G}^{-1}\big[G_I(k_x)\hat{U}-1\big],
      $$
      where $\hat{U}=V_{\mathrm{imp}}\tau_z\sigma_0$ is the impurity scattering matrix with scalar potential strength $V_{\mathrm{imp}}$, $\tau_z$ is the Pauli matrix in particle-hole (Nambu) space, $\sigma_0$ is the identity in spin space; $\tilde{G}=\frac{1}{\Omega_{\text{BZ}}}\int_{\text{BZ}} d^2p\,[H_{\mathrm{BdG}}(\mathbf{p})+H_Z]^{-2}$ (with $\Omega_{\text{BZ}}$ the area of the two-dimensional Brillouin zone, BZ, $H_{\mathrm{BdG}}(\mathbf{p})$ the bulk BdG Hamiltonian in momentum space, and $H_Z$ the Zeeman Hamiltonian) captures the onsite $E$-linear renormalization; and $G_I(k_x)=\sum_n G(0,\mathbf{r}_n)e^{-i a_0 n k_x}$ is the Fourier-transformed bulk Green function at zero energy evaluated at impurity sites $\mathbf{r}_n=n a_0\mathbf{e}_x$. The derivation proceeds from linearizing the bulk Green function in energy $E$, keeping the $O(E)$ term only on-site, yielding a nonlinear eigenproblem $\Psi = G(E)H_{\mathrm{imp}}\Psi$; after a supercell Fourier transform this reduces to $H_{\mathrm{eff}}(k_x)\Psi=E\Psi$. The mapping is exact for determining zero-energy gap closings (topological phase transitions) and provides a computationally efficient route to compute impurity-band dispersions, the effective pairing $\Delta_{\mathrm{eff}}(k_x)$ and effective dispersion $\xi_{\mathrm{eff}}(k_x)$, including longer-range couplings inherited from the two-dimensional lattice.

motivating_questions.content: Reliable phase-diagram mapping and parameter scans for realistic models require methods that are both accurate and computationally tractable. A validated reduced model that exactly captures zero-energy transition points and accurately estimates gaps is required to enable practical exploration of device parameters and to underpin experimental proposals with robust numerical evidence.

premises.content: An explicit tight-binding lattice Hamiltonian that realizes a topological nonsymmorphic crystalline insulator (TNCI) is constructed. The model has a layered antiferromagnetic structure with two sublattices A and B per unit cell displaced relative to each other so the surface $xz$ plane has the 2D nonsymmorphic wallpaper group $pmg$. Each site hosts three orbitals $|s\rangle$, $|p_x\rangle$, $|p_y\rangle$, and the full Hamiltonian is $H=H_A+H_B+H_{AB}$, with intralayer terms (for $\eta=A,B$) $H_{\eta}=\sum_{\langle\vec{n}\vec{m}\rangle_{in},\alpha\beta} t_{\vec{n}\vec{m}}^{\alpha\beta} c_{\alpha\vec{n}\eta}^\dagger c_{\beta\vec{m}\eta}+\sum_{\vec{n},\alpha}\epsilon_\alpha c_{\alpha\vec{n}\eta}^\dagger c_{\alpha\vec{n}\eta}+\sum_{\vec{n}}\delta_\eta M_1\left(-i c_{\vec{n}p_x\eta}^\dagger c_{\vec{n}p_y\eta}+\mathrm{H.c.}\right)$, and interlayer hopping $H_{AB}=\sum_{\langle\vec{n}\vec{m}\rangle_{AB},\alpha\beta}\left(r_{\vec{n}\vec{m}}^{\alpha\beta} c_{\alpha\vec{n}A}^\dagger c_{\beta\vec{m}B}+\mathrm{H.c.}\right)$. The nearest-neighbor intralayer hopping matrices in the basis $(|s\rangle,|p_x\rangle,|p_y\rangle)$ are $t_{\vec{n},\vec{n}+\hat{e}_x}=\begin{pmatrix} u_{s\sigma} & u_{sp\sigma} & 0 \\ -u_{sp\sigma} & u_{p\sigma} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & u_{p\pi} \end{pmatrix}$ and $t_{\vec{n},\vec{n}+\hat{e}_y}=\begin{pmatrix} u_{s\sigma} & 0 & u_{sp\sigma} \\ 0 & u_{p\pi} & 0 \\ -u_{sp\sigma} & 0 & u_{p\sigma} \end{pmatrix}$. The interlayer hopping matrix between A and B layers is $r_{\vec{n},\vec{n}+\hat{r}_0}=\begin{pmatrix} v_{s\sigma} & v_{sp\sigma}\lambda_1 & 0 \\ -v_{sp\sigma}\lambda_1 & v_{p\sigma}\lambda_1^2 + v_{p\pi}(1-\lambda_1^2) & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & v_{p\pi} \end{pmatrix}$, where $\lambda_1=2a_1/|\vec{r}_0|$ and $\vec{r}_0=\vec{r}_B-\vec{r}_A$. The Zeeman-like coupling $M_1$ acts on the $p$ orbitals and splits the $p_+$ and $p_-$ states (formed from $p_x$ and $p_y$). Under the $pmg$ symmetry constraints—mirror symmetry $\hat{m}_z$ requiring $H_{A(B)}(k_x,k_y,k_z)=H_{A(B)}(k_x,k_y,-k_z)$ and $H_{AB}(k_x,k_y,k_z)=H_{AB}(k_x,k_y,-k_z)$, glide symmetry $\hat{g}_x$ requiring $H_{A}(k_x,k_y,k_z)=m_x H_{B}(-k_x,k_y,k_z) m_x$ and $H_{AB}(k_x,k_y,k_z)=m_x H_{BA}(-k_x,k_y,k_z) m_x$ with $m_x=\mathrm{Diag}(1,-1,1)$, and the periodic boundary conditions $H_{A(B)}(\vec{k}+\vec{G})=H_{A(B)}(\vec{k})$ and $H_{AB}(\vec{k}+\vec{G})=e^{i\vec{G}\cdot\vec{r}_0} H_{AB}(\vec{k})$—the model exhibits the TNCI phase for $M_1$ in the interval approximately $(3.4,6.6)$.

premises.content: For systems whose surface (or $k_z$ plane) symmetry is the 2D nonsymmorphic wallpaper group $pmg$, occupied Bloch states can be grouped into symmetry-enforced two-state sets called "doublet pairs": if $|\phi_{\vec{\kappa}}^{I}\rangle$ is a common eigenstate of $H(\vec{\kappa})$ and mirror $\hat{m}_z$ at $\vec{\kappa}=(k_x,k_y,\pi/c)$, then $|\phi_{\hat{m}_x\vec{\kappa}}^{II}\rangle=e^{i\chi_{\vec{\kappa}}}\hat{g}_x|\phi_{\vec{\kappa}}^{I}\rangle$ forms its partner and the representations of $\hat{m}_z$ and $\hat{g}_x$ anticommute on this two-state subspace. Define the partial polarization for each member of the doublet pair as $P_\alpha(k_x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\oint dk_y\langle\phi_{\vec{k}}^{\alpha}| i\partial_{k_y}|\phi_{\vec{k}}^{\alpha}\rangle,\ \alpha=I,II$, which satisfy the relation $P_{II}(-k_x)=P_I(k_x)-\frac{1}{2\pi}(\chi_{\pi/a}-\chi_{-\pi/a})$. Using the non-Abelian Wilson-loop (Wannier center) approach, the sum of occupied Wannier centers yields the polarization $P=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{\text{occ}}\theta$, and the partner-switching (winding) of Wannier centers of doublet pairs around the $[-\pi,\pi)$ ring defines a $Z_2$ topological invariant. Equivalently, define the doublet polarization $P_d=P_I-P_{II}$ and the $Z_2$ invariant $\Delta = P_d(\pi)-P_d(0) \pmod{2}$.

steps.reasoning: Start from the explicit tight-binding model established earlier (conclusion with id="2") as given by $H=H_A+H_B+H_{AB}$ with the intralayer and interlayer blocks and the Zeeman-like $M_1$ coupling acting on $p$ orbitals; treat this model and its chosen numerical parameter set (see the parameter list) as the starting point for numerical investigation of phase transitions.

Start from the $Z_2$ topological invariant construction established earlier (conclusion with id="3"): accept as given that the $Z_2$ invariant can be computed by tracking the Wilson-loop (Wannier-center) eigenphase flows $\theta(k_x)$ for the occupied bands on the $k_z=\tfrac{\pi}{c}$ plane and that partner-switching (winding) parity of Wannier centers gives the invariant.

Specify the numerical parameter set used for the slab and bulk Wilson-loop calculations: use $u_{s\sigma}=-0.2$, $u_{sp\sigma}=0.2$, $u_{p\sigma}=0.2$, $u_{p\pi}=0.2$, $v_{s\sigma}=0.05$, $v_{sp\sigma}=0.3$, $v_{p\sigma}=-0.1$, $v_{p\pi}=0.1$, $\epsilon_s=0$, $\epsilon_p=-5$, $a=1$, $a_1=0.1$, and $c=2$ (the same parameter set used to obtain the phase diagram described in the paper).

Report the bulk gap closings and associate them with topological transitions as $M_1$ is varied: with the chosen parameters the bulk gap closes at three distinct values of the Zeeman-like parameter $M_1$, producing three notable events: (I) at $M_1=3.4$ the system transitions from topologically trivial to nontrivial, accompanied by the emergence of a single gapless surface Dirac cone at surface momentum $\bar{Z}$; (II) at $M_1=5.0$ the bulk gap closes but the $Z_2$ winding number remains unchanged because the gap closing occurs twice in a manner that preserves parity of winding; (III) at $M_1=6.6$ the system reenters the trivial phase, so the winding number reverts to the trivial value. These critical $M_1$ values are identified by locating points where the bulk gap vanishes in the computed bulk dispersion as a function of $M_1$.
Fig. 4

Report slab-spectrum evidence for surface-state appearance and location: compute the energy dispersion for a slab geometry with open boundary conditions along $y$ (so the surface normal is $\hat{y}$) and find that for $M_1=3.1$ (which is below the first critical value $3.4$) there are no surface states in the gap, whereas for $M_1=4.5$ (which lies between $3.4$ and $5.0$) a Dirac-type surface state appears centered at $\bar{Z}$ in the surface Brillouin zone; these slab spectral results corroborate that the phase for $M_1=4.5$ is topologically nontrivial with a single surface Dirac cone at $\bar{Z}$ while $M_1=3.1$ is trivial.
Fig. 2

Report Wilson-loop (Wannier-center) flow calculations that extract the bulk $Z_2$ invariant and track its changes across the transitions: calculate Wilson-loop eigenphases $\theta(k_x)$ for occupied bands on the $k_z=\tfrac{\pi}{c}$ plane and plot their evolution versus $k_x$; the flows show the winding-number sequence $0\to1\to0$ as $M_1$ is tuned through the critical values: just below $M_1=3.4$ the winding number is $0$ (trivial), just above $M_1=3.4$ the winding number is $1$ (nontrivial), around $M_1=5$ the winding number remains $1$ across the small gap closings (so there is no parity change), and above $M_1=6.6$ the winding number returns to $0$ (trivial); these flows are explicitly plotted and labeled with $M_1$ values in the paper to illustrate the three topological phase transitions.
Fig. 5

Combine slab-spectrum and Wilson-loop evidence to conclude the sequence of phases and critical $M_1$ values: the coincident observation of (i) the gap closing points at $M_1=3.4,5.0,6.6$ in bulk dispersion, (ii) the emergence/disappearance of Dirac surface states in slab spectra at values consistent with the Wannier-center winding changes (no surface states at $M_1=3.1$, Dirac surface state at $M_1=4.5$), and (iii) the Wilson-loop winding numbers changing parity as $M_1$ crosses $3.4$ and $6.6$ (but not across $5.0$), establishes numerically that the tight-binding model undergoes topological phase transitions at these $M_1$ values and that the nontrivial regime supports a single gapless Dirac surface state at $\bar{Z}$.

motivating_questions.content: Demonstrating a novel symmetry-protected topological phase requires concrete numerical evidence that (i) a bulk gap exists in parameter regimes, (ii) gapless surface states appear and are pinned at symmetry-determined surface momenta, and (iii) a bulk topological invariant changes across parameter-driven transitions. Prior to this work there were no explicit slab-band and Wilson-loop calculations for a model that breaks all antiunitary symmetries yet displays the required surface Dirac cones; without such numerical data one could not verify the correspondence between surface spectra and the proposed unitary-based Z_{2} invariant or locate the critical parameter regimes for band inversion.

steps.reasoning: The topological classification of the two end members is established by calculating the electronic structure with density functional theory (DFT), constructing a tight-binding Hamiltonian from Wannier functions, and evaluating the $Z_2$ invariants with the Wilson-loop method based on Wannier charge centers.
For antiferromagnetic $MnBi_2Te_4$, the calculated $Z_2$ invariant is $(1;000)$.
For $GeBi_2Te_4$, the calculated $Z_2$ invariant is $(1;001)$.
Because the two end members have different $Z_2$ indices within the same classification framework, they belong to different antiferromagnetic topological classes.

This distinction is necessary for interpreting the gap evolution under composition tuning, because a bulk gap closing can then correspond to a topological phase transition between distinct classes rather than a trivial band reshuffling.

motivating_questions.content: A bulk gap closing alone does not specify the nature of a topological phase transition, because materials in the same topological class can evolve without changing topology, while different classes require a transition. For the alloy series connecting $MnBi_2Te_4$ and $GeBi_2Te_4$, the crucial unresolved issue was whether the two endpoints are topologically distinct in a way that mandates a transition under composition tuning. Without explicit topological classification of both end members within the same framework, the observed gap evolution could not be interpreted unambiguously in terms of topological band theory.

conclusion.content:
Tight-binding numerical calculations on a cubic-lattice model of the three-dimensional topological insulator/s-wave superconductor (TI/SC) heterostructure (with parameters Dirac velocity $v$, quadratic band curvature $B$, band mass $m$, chemical potential $\mu$, and induced pairing amplitude $\Delta$) containing a vortex line of winding number one along $z$ show: (i) a change in the $Z_{2}$ topological invariant of the quasi-one-dimensional system at a critical chemical potential $\mu_{c}$ (where the renormalized mass $\widetilde{m}=m-Bk_{F}^{2}-\frac{B}{\xi^{2}}$ vanishes, with $k_{F}=\mu/v$ and $\xi=v/\Delta$) from $-1$ to $+1$, consistent with the prediction from the effective SSH-type Hamiltonian; (ii) the existence of vortex-bound bands and zero-energy modes localized at the ends of the vortex line in the topological regime $\mu<\mu_{c}$; and (iii) an oscillatory exponential decay of the finite-size energy splitting between the two end zero modes as a function of slab thickness $L_{z}$, which quantitatively agrees with the analytic expression
      $$
      \delta E=\frac{4\widetilde{m}v\mathcal{F}(k_{F}^{2}\xi^{2})}{\sqrt{4B\widetilde{m}-v^{2}}}\Big|\sin\!\Big(\frac{\sqrt{4\widetilde{m}B-v^{2}}}{2B}L_{z}\Big)\Big|\exp\!\Big(-\frac{vL_{z}}{2B}\Big),
      $$
      where $\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{F}(k_{F}^{2}\xi^{2})$ is a monotonic function of its argument.  Specifically, the splitting quickly saturates when the lateral sample dimensions satisfy $L_{x},L_{y}\gg\xi$, exhibits oscillations as a function of $L_{z}$ and $\mu$, and is suppressed in the large-$\mu$ (weak-pairing) limit ($k_{F}\xi\gg1$) due to the power-law decrease of the prefactor $\mathcal{F}(k_{F}^{2}\xi^{2})$.

premises.content:
For the three-dimensional topological insulator/s-wave superconductor (TI/SC) heterostructure with a vortex line of winding number one along the z-direction, projecting the effective Hamiltonian
      $$
      H_{\mathrm{eff}}=-\mathcal{F}(k_{F}^{2}\xi^{2})\left[\big(\widetilde{m}-B k_{z}^{2}\big)\nu_{z}+v k_{z}\nu_{y}\right],
      $$
      (where $k_{F}=\mu/v$, $\xi=v/\Delta$ is the superconducting coherence length, $\widetilde{m}=m-Bk_{F}^{2}-\frac{B}{\xi^{2}}$ is a renormalized mass parameter, $v$ is the Dirac velocity, $B$ is the quadratic band curvature, $\mathcal{F}$ is the function of $k_{F}^{2}\xi^{2}$ given by complete elliptic integrals) yields an analytic expression for the finite-thickness energy splitting $\delta E$ between the two end states of the vortex line,
      $$
      \delta E=\frac{4\widetilde{m}v\mathcal{F}(k_{F}^{2}\xi^{2})}{\sqrt{4B\widetilde{m}-v^{2}}}\Big|\sin\!\Big(\frac{\sqrt{4\widetilde{m}B-v^{2}}}{2B}L_{z}\Big)\Big|\exp\!\Big(-\frac{vL_{z}}{2B}\Big),
      $$
      where $L_{z}$ is the slab thickness.  The energy splitting decays exponentially in $L_{z}$ with decay length $\ell_{\mathrm{TI}}=\frac{2B}{v}$ set solely by the band curvature $B$ and the Dirac velocity $v$ (i.e., independent of the pairing amplitude $\Delta$) up to the overall prefactor $\mathcal{F}(k_{F}^{2}\xi^{2})$ and oscillates with an $L_{z}$-dependent phase governed by $\widetilde{m}$.  In the strong-pairing/small-$\mu$ limit ($k_{F}\xi\ll1$) $\mathcal{F}\simeq1$ and $\widetilde{m}\simeq m$, making $\ell_{\mathrm{TI}}$ purely an intrinsic TI length scale.  Thus the coherence length controlling inter-end Majorana hybridization in the TI/SC structure is anomalous in that it does not scale as the superconducting coherence length $\xi=v/\Delta$.

steps.reasoning: Specify the microscopic tight-binding model used for numerical simulations: the total lattice Hamiltonian is $\hat{H}_{\mathrm{tot}}=\hat{H}_{\mathrm{TI}}+\hat{H}_{\mathrm{SC}}+\hat{H}_{Z}$ defined on a cubic lattice, where $\hat{H}_{\mathrm{TI}}$ is the four-band lattice model describing the bulk topological insulator with orbital Pauli matrices $\rho_{i}$ and spin Pauli matrices $\sigma_{i}$ and parameters chosen so $2M/B$ lies in the strong TI regime; $\hat{H}_{\mathrm{SC}}$ implements proximity-induced pairing with vortex profile $\Delta(\mathbf{r})=\Delta_{0}f(z)\tanh(r_{\parallel}/\xi)$ and phase $\phi(\mathbf{r}_{\parallel})=\mathrm{Arg}(\mathbf{r}_{\parallel}-\mathbf{r}_{\parallel}^{0})$; and $\hat{H}_{Z}$ is an optional Zeeman exchange term restricted to top layers in the SMTI studies but absent for the TI/SC tight-binding calculations here. Parameter values used in representative figures are for example $\Delta=0.05$, $\hbar v=0.4$, $B=0.5$, $m=0.28$, and lattice sizes reported in figure captions. The authors use this tight-binding model both to compute the quasi-one-dimensional band structures and to obtain finite-size spectra and wavefunction profiles shown in the figures. [3]

Compute the $Z_{2}$ quasi-one-dimensional topological invariant $\nu$ numerically for the slab/vortex quasi-1D system as a function of $\mu$ by evaluating the product of the signs of Pfaffians of the antisymmetric real BdG Hamiltonians at time-reversal-invariant momenta $k_{z}=0,\pi$ (the numerical procedure is that used in the text), and observe a change of the invariant at a critical chemical potential $\mu=\mu_{c}$ consistent with the effective-model prediction that the vortex line undergoes a topological phase transition when the renormalized mass parameter vanishes; the authors present $\nu(\mu)$ (sign change at $\mu_{c}$) in the numerical plot. This establishes (i) in the conclusion. Fig. 1(b)[51]

Extract the quasi-1D band structure from the tight-binding calculations and identify vortex-bound bands: the numerically computed dispersions as a function of $k_{z}$ show bands whose radial probability distribution concentrates at the vortex core (indicated by a blue-to-red color gradient), with a pair of mid-gap vortex-bound bands (the darkest-blue dispersion in the figure) that appear when $\mu<\mu_{c}$; in the topological regime $\nu=-1$ corresponding to $\mu<\mu_{c}$ these vortex-bound bands yield end-localized zero-energy modes when open boundary conditions are imposed along $z$, confirming (ii) in the conclusion. Fig. 1(c)Fig. 1(d)

Compute finite-size spectra as a function of slab thickness $L_{z}$ (implemented as $N_{z}$ lattice layers) using the tight-binding model with lateral dimensions $L_{x},L_{y}$, and show that (a) the splitting of the two end states decays exponentially with $L_{z}$ and oscillates as $L_{z}$ varies, reproducing the oscillatory exponential form derived analytically, (b) the splitting saturates with respect to lateral sizes once $L_{x},L_{y}\gg\xi$, demonstrating that lateral confinement does not control the hybridization when the lateral dimensions exceed the superconducting coherence length $\xi$, and (c) the oscillation phase and amplitude depend on $\mu$, in agreement with the analytic formula which predicts a $\mu$-dependent renormalized mass and a $\sin(\cdot L_{z})$ factor; these numerical behaviors are displayed in the plots of energy versus $N_{z}$ and energy versus $\mu$, corroborating the analytic expression quantitatively. Fig. 1(f)Fig. 1(g)

Demonstrate suppression of the finite-size splitting in the large-$\mu$ / weak-pairing regime: numerically vary $\mu$ and pairing amplitude parameters to reach $k_{F}\xi\gg1$ and observe that the finite-size induced splitting amplitude becomes strongly suppressed, consistent with the analytic asymptotic form $\mathcal{F}(k_{F}^{2}\xi^{2})\simeq\dfrac{\ln(4k_{F}\xi)-1}{k_{F}^{2}\xi^{2}}$ in that limit; the authors explicitly state that the numerics show suppression of splitting for large $\mu$, matching the analytic prefactor dependence.

motivating_questions.content: Analytic projection and continuum approximations can leave open questions about finite-lattice and full-BdG effects (e.g., regularization at large momenta, discretization and finite lateral size).  Numerical tight-binding simulations are therefore required to (a) verify the existence and localization of end states in realistic finite geometries with a vortex, (b) confirm the exponential-$L_{z}$ decay and oscillatory behavior predicted analytically, and (c) check parameter regimes (finite $\mu$, finite $\Delta$, finite lateral sizes) where the analytic approximations remain accurate.  The numerics validate that the coherence-length anomaly is not an artifact of projection approximations but appears in the full lattice BdG spectrum.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: For (001) surfaces there exist two inequivalent surface terminations arising from the two-sublattice choices: the “[110]-ribbed” termination obtained by choosing unit-cell indices $\mu=0$ or $\mu=3$, and the orthogonal “[{\bar 1}10]-ribbed” termination obtained by choosing $\mu=1$ or $\mu=2$. The computed winding number $w(\mathbf{k}_{\parallel})$ is nonzero on complementary regions of the (001) surface Brillouin zone for these two terminations: where one termination has $w\neq 0$ the other has $w=0$, and vice versa. Correspondingly, tight-binding band-structure calculations for finite-thickness slabs show zero-energy surface-flat bands (surface-localized states) appearing precisely in the regions where $w(\mathbf{k}_{\parallel})\neq 0$ for the chosen termination.

conclusion.content: In the nearest-neighbor tight-binding model on the diamond lattice with chiral symmetry, the unit-cell choice indexed by $\mu$ ($\mu=0,1,2,3$) corresponds to the four possible ways to pair an A-sublattice site with a B-sublattice site as the basis, with vectors $\mathbf{a}_i^{(\mu)} = \boldsymbol{\delta}_\mu - \boldsymbol{\delta}_i$ connecting A-B sites. For (001) surfaces, with surface-parallel wavevector $\mathbf{k}_{\parallel} = (k_x', k_y')$ where $k_x'$ along [110] and $k_y'$ along [1-10], and perpendicular momentum $k_{\perp} = k_z$ with 1D lattice constant $\tilde a = a/2$, the winding number $w(\mathbf{k}_{\parallel})$ is computed from the bulk off-diagonal Hamiltonian components $h_x^{(\mu)}(\mathbf{k}) = t\sum_i \cos(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{a}_i^{(\mu)})$ and $h_y^{(\mu)}(\mathbf{k}) = t\sum_i \sin(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{a}_i^{(\mu)})$ via the integral $w(\mathbf{k}_{\parallel}) = \int_0^{2\pi/\tilde a} \frac{dk_{\perp}}{2\pi} [\hat{h}_x \partial_{k_{\perp}} \hat{h}_y - \hat{h}_y \partial_{k_{\perp}} \hat{h}_x]$ with $\hat{\mathbf{h}} = \mathbf{h}/|\mathbf{h}|$. There exist two inequivalent surface terminations: the "[110]-ribbed" termination obtained by choosing $\mu=0$ or $\mu=3$, and the orthogonal "[{\bar 1}10]-ribbed" termination obtained by choosing $\mu=1$ or $\mu=2$. The computed winding number $w(\mathbf{k}_{\parallel})$ is nonzero on complementary regions of the (001) surface Brillouin zone for these two terminations: where one termination has $w\neq 0$ the other has $w=0$, and vice versa. Correspondingly, tight-binding band-structure calculations for finite-thickness slabs (thickness 40 sites perpendicular) show zero-energy surface-flat bands (surface-localized states) appearing precisely in the regions where $w(\mathbf{k}_{\parallel})\neq 0$ for the chosen termination.
conclusion.metadata: {"narrative": "Conclusion 2's claim that (001) surfaces have two inequivalent terminations with complementary surface-state regions rests on two pillars: the winding-number maps (Fig. 6) and the slab band-structure calculations (Fig. 7). P2 points out that the winding-number argument is weakened by the unresolved gap condition for (001) surface: the projection of the bulk nodal line onto the (001) SBZ is not computed, so it is unknown whether the w\u22600 regions overlap with gapless points. This formal risk (P2) is significant if it turns out that some of the claimed surface-state regions coincide with the nodal-line projection. However, highlight H1 provides strong direct evidence from slab calculations that the surface states appear exactly in the predicted regions for both terminations. This numerical verification is independent of the formal gap condition and, together with the agreement with the BB(001) flat-band result from Hirashima (2016) noted in H1, supports the conclusion with high credibility. P2 remains as a caveat about the topological protection of those states, but the existence and termination-dependence of the surface states are well-established by the slab data."}

The index theorem that links a nonzero $w$ to the existence of zero-energy surface states requires the 1D subsystem at each fixed $\mathbf{k}_{\parallel}$ to have a non-zero gap: $|\mathbf{h}^{(\mu)}(k_x', k_y', k_z)| > 0$ for all $k_z$. The diamond lattice bulk has a nodal line along the X–W direction; its projection onto the (001) surface Brillouin zone is not computed. Consequently, it is not verified that the $\mathbf{k}_{\parallel}$ regions where $w(\mathbf{k}_{\parallel}) \neq 0$ for the [110]-ribbed and [1-10]-ribbed terminations lie entirely outside this projection; for $\mathbf{k}_{\parallel}$ that fall on the projection, the winding number is ill-defined and the associated surface states may not be topologically protected by the chiral winding number.[Original citation text, unchanged]

premises.content: For the diamond lattice tight-binding model (nearest-neighbor hopping t) with (001) surfaces and finite thickness (40 layers), the band structure computed along high-symmetry lines of the surface Brillouin zone shows zero-energy flat bands concentrated in the SBZ regions where the winding number w(k_x',k_y') was computed to be nonzero (shaded regions in Fig. 6) for both the [110]-ribbed (μ=0 or 3) and [1-10]-ribbed (μ=1 or 2) terminations. The surface states are absent in the SBZ regions where w=0. The complementary coverage of the two terminations is also evident: the union of the shaded regions from the two maps covers the entire SBZ, matching the known fully flat BB(001) surfaces (Hirashima 2016).

premises.content:
For the nearest-neighbor tight-binding model on the bipartite diamond lattice with unit-cell choice indexed by $\mu$, define the bulk off-diagonal Hamiltonian components
      $h_{x}^{(\mu)}(\mathbf{k})=t\sum_{i}\cos\big(\mathbf{k}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{a}_{i}^{(\mu)}\big)$ and
      $h_{y}^{(\mu)}(\mathbf{k})=t\sum_{i}\sin\big(\mathbf{k}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{a}_{i}^{(\mu)}\big)$,
      where $t$ is the nearest-neighbor hopping and $\mathbf{a}_{i}^{(\mu)}$ are the vectors connecting A- and B-sublattice sites in the chosen unit cell. For a fixed surface-parallel wavevector $\mathbf{k}_{\parallel}$, treat the remaining momentum $k_{\perp}$ (normal to the surface) as the 1D Brillouin-zone variable with lattice constant $\tilde a$; define the normalized vector $\hat{\mathbf{h}}^{(\mu)}(\mathbf{k})=\mathbf{h}^{(\mu)}(\mathbf{k})/|\mathbf{h}^{(\mu)}(\mathbf{k})|$ with $\mathbf{h}^{(\mu)}(\mathbf{k})=[h_x^{(\mu)}(\mathbf{k}),h_y^{(\mu)}(\mathbf{k})]$. Then the integer winding number
      $$
      w(\mathbf{k}_{\parallel})=\int_{0}^{2\pi/\tilde a}\frac{dk_{\perp}}{2\pi}\Big[\hat{h}_{x}^{(\mu)}(\mathbf{k})\frac{\partial}{\partial k_{\perp}}\hat{h}_{y}^{(\mu)}(\mathbf{k})-\hat{h}_{y}^{(\mu)}(\mathbf{k})\frac{\partial}{\partial k_{\perp}}\hat{h}_{x}^{(\mu)}(\mathbf{k})\Big]
      $$
      characterizes the 1D subsystem at fixed $\mathbf{k}_{\parallel}$. A nonzero value of $w(\mathbf{k}_{\parallel})$ predicts the existence of a zero-energy surface-localized state for that $\mathbf{k}_{\parallel}$ in the chiral-symmetric nearest-neighbor diamond-lattice model; conversely, $w(\mathbf{k}_{\parallel})=0$ predicts absence of such a protected zero mode in the limit of open boundary perpendicular to $k_{\perp}$.

steps.reasoning: Start from the winding-number criterion established above as a known starting point: the integer $w(\mathbf{k}_{\parallel})$ computed from the bulk off-diagonal Hamiltonian components $h_{x}^{(\mu)}(\mathbf{k})$ and $h_{y}^{(\mu)}(\mathbf{k})$ determines whether a zero-energy boundary-localized state exists for that surface-parallel momentum $\mathbf{k}_{\parallel}$.

Identify the two inequivalent (001) surface terminations and their corresponding unit-cell gauges: define unit-cell index $\mu$ and state that the surface structure labeled "[110]-ribbed" is obtained by choosing $\mu=0$ or $\mu=3$, while the orthogonal surface labeled "$[\bar{1}10]$-ribbed" is obtained by choosing $\mu=1$ or $\mu=2$. Reference the surface-structure illustrations that depict these two terminations. Fig. 5

Specify the surface-parallel and surface-normal wavevector coordinates used to compute the winding number for (001) surfaces: define $\mathbf{k}_{\parallel}=(k_{x}^{\prime},k_{y}^{\prime})$ with $k_{x}^{\prime}$ along the $[110]$ direction and $k_{y}^{\prime}$ along the $[\bar{1}10]$ direction, define the perpendicular momentum $k_{\perp}=k_{z}$ which is normal to the (001) surface, and set the one-dimensional lattice constant $\tilde{a}=a/2$ for the (001) effective 1D Brillouin zone (where $a$ is the fcc lattice constant).

State the computed behavior of the winding number across the (001) surface Brillouin zone: the winding number $w(\mathbf{k}_{\parallel})$ is nonzero only in a part of the surface Brillouin zone for a given termination, and the regions are complementary between the two inequivalent terminations — specifically, where the [110]-ribbed termination has $w(\mathbf{k}_{\parallel})\neq 0$, the $[\bar{1}10]$-ribbed termination has $w(\mathbf{k}_{\parallel})=0$, and vice versa. This complementary pattern is presented graphically for the two terminations. Fig. 6

Connect the bulk topological calculation to finite-thickness numerical spectra: tight-binding band-structure calculations for finite-thickness slabs with (001) surfaces (slabs terminated according to the chosen unit-cell gauge) show zero-energy surface-flat bands that appear precisely in the regions of the (001) surface Brillouin zone where the computed $w(\mathbf{k}_{\parallel})\neq 0$ for that termination; conversely, no zero-energy surface bands are observed where $w(\mathbf{k}_{\parallel})=0$. The numerical slab band structures illustrating this agreement are displayed. Fig. 7

Record the additional remark connecting to previous work: surfaces that combine the two complementary terminations (denoted BB(001) in prior work) yield a completely flat zero-energy band across the entire surface Brillouin zone because one or the other termination provides $w(\mathbf{k}_{\parallel})\neq 0$ at every $\mathbf{k}_{\parallel}$; this observation is reported in earlier work and discussed in the paper. motivating_questions.content: Prior studies reported surface states for specific (001)-type terminations but did not map how inequivalent sublattice terminations for the same macroscopic (001) normal populate the entire surface Brillouin zone. In particular, earlier work presented completely flat bands for certain combinations of terminations but did not explain why some single-termination slabs exhibit surface states only over part of the SBZ and why the complementary termination yields surface states in the complementary SBZ region. This left unclear how to predict, from the bulk Hamiltonian and a particular unit-cell choice conforming to the termination, where in the (001) SBZ zero-energy surface states will occur.

premises.content:
To reproduce the time-reversal-invariant $\mathbb{Z}_2$ lattice Hamiltonian
      $$
      \mathcal{H}=\sum_{m,n}\lambda_{m,n}\mathbf{c}_{m,n}^{\dagger}\mathbf{c}_{m,n}-t_0\sum_{m,n}\left(\mathbf{c}_{m+1,n}^{\dagger}e^{i\hat{\theta}_x}\mathbf{c}_{m,n}+\mathbf{c}_{m,n+1}^{\dagger}e^{i\hat{\theta}_y}\mathbf{c}_{m,n}+\mathrm{H.c.}\right),
      $$
      with $\mathbf{c}_{m,n}=(c_{m,n,\uparrow},c_{m,n,\downarrow})^T$, $\hat{\theta}_x=2\pi\alpha y\sigma_z$, $\hat{\theta}_y=2\pi\beta\sigma_x$, and staggered on-site potential $\lambda_{m,n}=(-1)^n\lambda$, choose the effective nearest-neighbor coefficients in the derived tight-binding model as follows. For the $x$-direction hopping between site $(m,n)$ and $(m+1,n)$ set the spin-preserving hoppings
      $$
      t_{0,((m+1)n),(m,n),\uparrow\uparrow}=t_{0,((m+1)n),(m,n),\downarrow\downarrow}=t_0,
      $$
      with the site-dependent Peierls phases
      $$
      \varphi_{((m+1)n),(m,n),\uparrow\uparrow}=2n\pi\alpha,\qquad \varphi_{((m+1)n),(m,n),\downarrow\downarrow}=-2n\pi\alpha.
      $$
      For the $y$-direction hopping between $(m,n)$ and $(m,n+1)$ set all four spin-resolved hoppings equal to $t_0$ with a common phase $2\pi\beta$,
      $$
      t_{0,(m,(n+1)),(m,n),\eta\eta'}=t_0,\qquad \varphi_{(m,(n+1)),(m,n),\eta\eta'}=2\pi\beta\quad(\eta,\eta'=\uparrow,\downarrow).
      $$
      Setting all other effective coupling coefficients to zero reproduces the lattice Hamiltonian above and thus realizes a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-class model that supports the quantum spin Hall effect; in the superconducting-circuit implementation these assignments identify which resonant multi-tone components and their amplitudes and phases must be programmed into each link's time-dependent coupling $J_{\mathbf{r r}'}(t)$ to generate the spin-dependent Peierls phases $\hat{\theta}_x$ and $\hat{\theta}_y$.

motivating_questions.content: Having a controllable circuit implementation of the target Hamiltonian still leaves the question of which parameter ranges realize a topological insulator versus a trivial/metallic state. Prior experimental platforms lacked a concrete experimentally-realizable phase diagram for a spinful $\mathbb{Z}_2$ model with independently tunable spin-mixing $\beta$ and staggered potential $\lambda$. A computed phase diagram is necessary to (i) identify parameter regimes to target in experiment, (ii) choose Fermi energies where edge states are expected, and (iii) demonstrate that tuning $\beta$ and $\lambda$ can drive topological phase transitions in the concrete simulator.
